evidence.claim: The Forest Heritage National Scenic Byway winds through Pisgah National Forest on 17.6 miles of US 276.
evidence.quote: Forest Heritage National Scenic Byway National Scenic Byway • North Carolina Length 17.6 mi / 28.3 km

evidence.claim: It climbs Pisgah Ridge, crosses the Blue Ridge Parkway and turns through switchbacks above the Pink Beds, an upland bog of rhododendrons and laurels.
evidence.quote: Crossing back into Transylvania County at Wagon Road Gap (el. 4,528 ft (1,380 m)), it connects again with the Blue Ridge Parkway before making a switchback descent into the Pink Beds.

evidence.claim: an upland bog of rhododendrons and laurels.
evidence.quote: The Pink Beds is an upland bog with dense growth of pink blooming rhododendrons and laurels.

evidence.claim: The Federal Highway Administration presents the drive as a way to understand forest history through old settlement roads, mountain peaks and waterfalls.
evidence.quote: As you wind your way on old settlement roads past mountain peaks and cascading waterfalls, imagine how this landscape looked decades ago when modern forestry began.

evidence.claim: This national section is part of a longer National Forest Scenic Byway loop using NC 215, US 276 and US 64.
evidence.quote: The National Forest Scenic Byway is the longest and makes a loop along NC 215, US 276 and US 64

evidence.claim: Some of those road cuts began as logging railways.
evidence.quote: These old cuts now form the path for some stretches of the byway.

evidence.claim: After buying timber rights from George Vanderbilt, Louis Carr laid tracks along creeks to carry out wood.
evidence.quote: When Louis Carr purchased the rights to “all timber, wood and bark standing and down” from Vanderbilt, he built rail lines along creeks to bring out the timber.

evidence.claim: The landscape also became a classroom for Carl Schenck’s Biltmore Forest School, where students learned forest management through fieldwork.
evidence.quote: Schenck's students spent most afternoons in the forest doing hands-on work and directly applying the theories they had learned in the classroom.

evidence.claim: The wider Forest Heritage route gained Forest Service designation in 1989; this US 276 section became a National Scenic Byway in 2009.
evidence.quote: The Forest Heritage Scenic Byway was established in 1989 as a United States Forest Service (USFS); in 1990, it also became a North Carolina Scenic Byway. In 2009, part of US 276 portion of the scenic byway was also designated as a National Scenic Byway

evidence.claim: Driving south from Shining Creek Gap, climb to Wagon Road Gap, then descend into the Pink Beds and the Cradle of Forestry.
evidence.quote: At Shining Creek Gap (el. 3,671 ft (1,119 m)) is where the Shining Rock Trail Head is located and the beginning of the National Scenic Byway;

evidence.claim: Driving south from Shining Creek Gap, climb to Wagon Road Gap, then descend into the Pink Beds and the Cradle of Forestry.
evidence.quote: the scenic byway now quickly climbs up the Pisgah Ridge again. Crossing back into Transylvania County at Wagon Road Gap

evidence.claim: the Cradle of Forestry.
evidence.quote: Located nearby is the Cradle of Forestry

evidence.claim: Sliding Rock follows, then Looking Glass Falls.

evidence.claim: Sliding Rock follows, then Looking Glass Falls.
evidence.quote: En route, you will pass Looking Glass Falls and the parking area for Moore Cove Falls.

evidence.claim: Near Brevard, two stone pillars mark the forest boundary and honor Transylvania County residents who served in World War I.
evidence.quote: a pair of stone pillars, which were built to honor Transylvania County residents who served in World War I and also mark the border of the Pisgah National Forest.

evidence.claim: The national byway ends at US 64 and NC 280.
evidence.quote: At the intersection of US 64/US 276 and NC 280, both the North Carolina Scenic Byway and National Scenic Byway ends;

evidence.claim: Carl Schenck’s forestry students learned their trade in the woods as well as the classroom.
evidence.quote: Schenck's students spent most afternoons in the forest doing hands-on work and directly applying the theories they had learned in the classroom.

evidence.claim: His early classrooms occupied abandoned farm buildings on Vanderbilt’s estate.
evidence.quote: Schenck established the Biltmore Forest School in 1896 using abandoned farm buildings on the estate grounds

evidence.claim: They felled trees, operated machinery, transplanted seedlings and tended nurseries.
evidence.quote: The students learned felling, logging, sawing, operating machinery, transplanting seedlings, and caring for tree nurseries.

evidence.claim: Schenck had come from Germany in 1895 to manage George Vanderbilt’s forests, then began teaching volunteers who helped with the work.
evidence.quote: In 1895, George W. Vanderbilt brought Carl A. Schenck from Germany to the Biltmore Estate in western North Carolina to manage the vast expanses of forest lands on the estate's property.

evidence.claim: then began teaching volunteers who helped with the work.
evidence.quote: using local young men and other volunteers who were interested in working for free as an apprentice.

evidence.claim: The Biltmore Forest School became North America’s first forestry school.
evidence.quote: The Biltmore Forest School was the first school of forestry in North America.

evidence.claim: Its former grounds are now the Cradle of Forestry in America, with exhibits on forestry and conservation.
evidence.quote: The school grounds are now part of Pisgah National Forest in Transylvania County, North Carolina, as the Cradle of Forestry in America, a 6,500 acres (2,600 ha) historic site which features exhibits about forestry and forest conservation history.

evidence.claim: A 1914 logging locomotive and a portable sawmill give that practical education a material presence.
evidence.quote: a 1914 Climax logging locomotive, and a portable sawmill.

evidence.claim: Looking Glass Creek makes a sloping slide here, about 60 feet long, ending in a deep pool.
evidence.quote: It has a gentle slope and is about 60 feet long, ending in a large, deep pool

evidence.claim: The water stays near 55°F year round.
evidence.quote: The water in the river and the plunge pool remains near 55 degrees Fahrenheit year round.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service developed the natural slide into a recreation area, now managed by Adventure Pisgah.
evidence.quote: The area has been developed by the US Forest Service into a popular recreation area. The area is currently being managed by a company called Adventure Pisgah

evidence.claim: A viewing platform provides a place to watch; a lower platform was destroyed by flooding in 2021.
